channel.title: Massachusetts and RI Lawyers Weekly - Article Feed
channel.description: Latest articles from Massachusetts and RI Lawyers Weekly (masslawyersweekly.com)

item.title: Lawyers of the Year: Kerry L. Timbers
item.description: Last year brought a major victory for intellectual property litigator Kerry L. Timbers in a case that began back in 2018.

item.title: Lawyers of the Year: Max D. Stern and William Gildea
item.description: Max D. Stern and William Gildea made an indelible mark on 2025 when they prevailed in a bitter, headline-grabbing feud between two high-ranking state officials.

item.title: Lawyers of the Year: Matthew C. Moschella
item.description: When he joined Sherin & Lodgen in 2004 as an associate, one of the first cases Matthew C. Moschella worked on was the death row appeal of Anthony Boyd, an Alabama man convicted for his role in the 1993 murder of Gregory Huguley.

item.title: Lawyers of the Year: David Milton and Kayla H. Ghantous
item.description: It may go down as the most expensive case of misdirected anger in the history of the Massachusetts prison system.

item.title: Lawyers of the Year: Dawn M. Mertineit
item.description: When the Massachusetts Noncompetition Agreement Act, which limits the use of noncompetes in the commonwealth, took effect in 2018, many in the employment bar believed it applied exclusively to noncompetes and not to other restrictive covenants.

item.title: Lawyers of the Year: Shira M. Diner
item.description: The tension had been simmering in the criminal justice system for years. Then, around Memorial Day last year, bar advocates turned up the heat, declining to accept new cases until their pay rates were brought more in line with their peers in other states.

item.title: Lawyers of the Year: David E. Cherny
item.description: Does the Probate & Family Court have the power to make changes to an erroneous voluntary acknowledgement of paternity after the statute of repose has lapsed? No, the Supreme Judicial Court declared in 2025.

item.title: Lawyers of the Year: Jeffrey N. Catalano and Jonathan D. Sweet
item.description: The underlying facts of the case made headlines nationwide, and in 2025 the Supreme Judicial Court added to the coverage when it held that families who donated the bodies of their loved ones for research only to learn that they may have met a grisly fate can sue Harvard Medical School.

item.title: Lawyers of the Year: Lisa Brodeur-McGan, Katharine E. Shove-Harrington And Danielle L. McGan
item.description: Three Westfield attorneys made a powerful statement for reform in the Massachusetts State Police by securing a multi-million-dollar employment discrimination verdict on behalf of officers who claimed they were denied desirable specialty unit positions because of their race and/or gender.

item.title: Lawyers of the Year 2025
item.description: A special section profiling the work of 15 attorneys who made headlines in the legal community last year.
